title: Not by birth (383–390)
hookLine: not by birth is one a brahmana, but by conduct; cut the stream, be bold

cards: Old money. Good family. A title you inherit.
Every society has words of honor that come with a family name. Yet a person with every advantage of birth can behave badly, and a person with none of them can be simply noble.
The last chapter of the Dhammapada takes a word of honor from its world and asks a sharp question: what actually earns it? Verse after verse in it ends the same way.

teach.b: Today's word is brahmana, in Sanskrit brahmin.

In the Buddha's India, brahmins were the hereditary priestly class, keepers of the Vedas and the sacred rites, and many were honored teachers; in the suttas, brahmins come to the Buddha as questioners, and some become his students.
In these verses the word stays a word of honor. What changes is what it takes to earn it.
In the discourse on the outcast, he puts it directly: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. By deeds one becomes an outcast, and by deeds one becomes a brahmin.

The Dhammapada's last chapter is built on that idea. It opens with courage: cut off the stream of craving, be bold, drive away desire. When you understand how things come to an end, it says, you know the unmade.
The sun shines by day, the moon by night, the warrior in armor, the brahmana in meditation; but the Buddha shines day and night.
And a verse full of wordplay: one is called a brahmana for having put evil away, a samana, a renunciant, for living in calm, and a pabbajita, one gone forth, for sending his own impurities away.
The refrain runs through all four days of this chapter: him I call a brahmana.
Each verse fills it with conduct: patience, gentleness, truth, freedom from clinging. Nobility, in this chapter, is something you do.

how: Buddhist teachers use the brahmana chapter and the Vasala Sutta to teach that worth comes from conduct, not birth; in Theravada countries the chapter's verses are often chanted, and its refrain is well known.

o: a title of honor earned by conduct, not birth
a merchant's rank earned by trade and wealth
a warrior sworn to protect the king and land

games.q: match each word in today's verses.
p: in this chapter, earned by conduct

s: the Buddha threw away the word brahmana
he kept it as a word of honor and said it's earned by deeds.
the Vasala Sutta says birth makes a brahmin
it says by deeds one becomes a brahmin, and by deeds an outcast.
in the suttas, brahmins come to the Buddha as questioners
and some stay on as his students.

games.q: someone of high birth behaves cruelly; someone of low birth behaves nobly. who does this chapter call a brahmana?
o: neither; it depends on their family.
games.why: the Buddha said no one is a brahmin by birth; by deeds one becomes a brahmin.

practice: Let go, for these two minutes, of every label that came with you: your family name, your job title, where you're from, what you own; none of them are needed to breathe. Notice what's left: this breath, this body, this attention.
Then picture one small, good thing you could do that nobody will ever know about, and rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Brahmana. In the Buddha's world a priestly class by birth; in this chapter, a title earned only by conduct.

orig.note: Pali brāhmaṇa (Sanskrit brāhmaṇa, 'brahmin'): chapter twenty-six's title and refrain.

carryVoice: Your line: nobility is something you do. Birth hands out names; deeds earn them. See you tomorrow.
